TRUTH.title: The no-yes-man prompt
TRUTH.intro: Most AI assistants agree with you the moment you push back, even when you're wrong. Paste this at the start of a chat (or into your custom instructions) and it will tell you when you're wrong.

prompts.name: Paste at the start of any chat
prompts.text:
For this whole conversation, be an honest expert, not a cheerleader.
- If I say something wrong, tell me plainly and explain why, even if I push back.
- Don't open with praise like "Great question" or "You're absolutely right".
- When you're not sure, say how sure you are (for example: about 70% sure) and what would change your mind.
- If I disagree with you, only change your answer if I give you a new fact or a better argument. Repeating myself is not a reason.
Reply "Understood" and wait for my first question.

prompts.name: The 2-second test
prompts.text: I think [your claim]. Before you answer, list the 3 strongest reasons I might be wrong, then give your honest verdict in one line.

TRUTH.tip: Try it with a wrong fact on purpose. A good setup says "No, and here's why".

HUMAN.title: Sound like you, not like AI
HUMAN.intro: The words that give AI writing away, and a prompt that rewrites any text so it sounds like a person wrote it.

prompts.name: The rewrite prompt
prompts.text:
Rewrite the text below so it sounds like me talking to a colleague.
Rules:
- Short sentences. Contractions (I'm, don't, it's).
- No dashes of any kind. Use full stops or commas.
- Never use these words: delve, tapestry, testament, leverage, seamless, robust, elevate, embark, realm, journey, navigate, crucial, pivotal, foster, unlock, in today's fast-paced world, I hope this email finds you well, warm regards, furthermore, moreover.
- No intro, no summary at the end, no bullet points unless I had them.
- Keep my meaning and my facts. Don't add anything new.
Text:
[paste here]

prompts.name: Your voice, saved
prompts.text: Here are 3 messages I wrote myself: [paste 3 of your own emails or texts]. Describe my writing style in 5 short rules. From now on, write everything for me using those rules.

HUMAN.tip: The fastest check: read it out loud. If you wouldn't say it, cut it.

SHORT.title: Short answers, every time
SHORT.intro: Asked for one line and got five headings and a table? These two prompts fix that for good.

prompts.name: Put this in your custom instructions
prompts.text: Answer in the fewest words that fully answer the question. Default to 1 to 3 sentences. No headings, tables or bullet points unless I ask. No "Great question", no summary at the end, and don't offer to expand. If the question truly needs more, give the short answer first, then ask if I want detail.

prompts.name: For one question
prompts.text: Answer in one sentence of under 20 words. No preamble. [your question]

SHORT.tip: Custom instructions live in your AI app's settings (often called Personalisation or Instructions). Set it once and every chat follows it.

FIX.title: Change only what I asked
FIX.intro: Asked your AI to fix one typo and it rewrote everything? This prompt keeps it on a leash.

prompts.name: The surgical edit
prompts.text:
Make ONLY this change: [describe the change].
Do not change any other word, line, format or punctuation.
Return the full text with the change made, then list exactly what you changed as: line, before, after.
If you think something else should change, tell me after the list instead of doing it.
Text:
[paste here]

prompts.name: Check its work
prompts.text: Compare your version with my original word by word. List every difference. If there is any difference I didn't ask for, undo it and give me the corrected version.

FIX.tip: Works for CVs, code, captions and emails. The "list what you changed" line is what keeps it honest.

MEMORY.title: Make it stop repeating the mistake
MEMORY.intro: It says sorry, then does the same thing again. Here's how to give your AI a rule it actually keeps.

prompts.name: A rules block for the start of a chat
prompts.text:
Before you answer anything in this chat, read these rules. Check every answer against them before you send it.
RULES:
1. My name is spelled [Meera]. Never [Mira].
2. [your rule]
3. [your rule]
At the end of each answer, write "Rules checked". If you broke one, fix it before sending.

prompts.name: When it gets it wrong again
prompts.text: You made the same mistake again: [mistake]. Don't apologise. Quote the rule you broke, explain in one line why it happened, then give the corrected version.

MEMORY.tip: Long chats make AI forget early instructions. If a chat gets long, start a new one and paste the rules block first.

MUM.title: AI words, explained for Mum and Papa
MUM.intro: Ten AI words your parents keep hearing, each in one line they'll actually understand. Send this to the family group.

prompts.name: The cheat sheet
prompts.text:
PROMPT: your order. Like at a tea stall: "cutting chai, less sugar, extra ginger" gets you exactly that. Clearer order, better answer.
TOKEN: the AI reads in small pieces, like puris. Every piece is counted. Long messages use more.
HALLUCINATION: the AI makes something up and sounds sure, like the uncle at every wedding. Always double check facts, medicines and money.
MEMORY: in a long chat it forgets the start, like a family group with 300 unread messages. Start a new chat and say who you are.
MODEL: the cook. Same kitchen, different cook, different taste.
AGENT: an AI that can also press the buttons: book, send, pay. Only let it do what you'd let a stranger do.
DEEPFAKE: a fake video or voice that looks and sounds real.
VOICE CLONE: a fake call that sounds like your son or daughter asking for money. Hang up and call them back on their real number.
TRAINING: how the AI learned, by reading a huge library of text.
CHATBOT: the app you type to, like the one you're using.

prompts.name: Ask your AI to explain anything like this
prompts.text: Explain [AI word] to my 60-year-old mother in 2 sentences, using an everyday Indian example. No English jargon.

MUM.tip: The voice clone line is the one that matters most. Make sure they read that one.

SHOP.title: 5 prompts to run a small shop with AI
SHOP.intro: The five jobs the committee did for Mitti this week, as prompts you can use for your own shop, whatever you sell.

prompts.name: 1. Price it
prompts.text: I sell [product] made from [materials]. It costs me [cost] to make and takes [time]. Similar products sell for [prices you've seen]. My buyers are [who]. Suggest 3 prices (budget, fair, premium) with one line on who each one is for. Be honest if my cost is too high.

prompts.name: 2. The product description
prompts.text: Write a product description for [product] in under 40 words. Say what it is, who it's for and one detail that makes it different. No fancy words. Then give me 3 short titles.

prompts.name: 3. The post that sells
prompts.text: Write 3 short Instagram captions to sell [product] for [festival or occasion]. Each under 25 words, with one clear reason to buy now. No hashtag walls, max 3 hashtags.

prompts.name: 4. Answer the customer
prompts.text: A customer asked: "[their message]". Our real facts: [delivery time, price, stock]. Write a friendly reply under 40 words. Only promise what's in our facts.

prompts.name: 5. The review reply
prompts.text: Write a warm, short reply to this review: "[review]". Thank them by name, mention one detail from the review, no discount offers.

SHOP.tip: Prompt 4 is the one that saves you: "only promise what's in our facts" stops the AI inventing free gift wrap.

SAFE.title: The family safety message (AI scams)
SAFE.intro: Fake calls in your child's voice and fake videos of famous people are real now. Send this to your parents and agree a code word on the phone, never in the comments.

prompts.name: Send this to the family group
prompts.text:
Important, please read 🙏
Scammers can now copy our voices with AI and make fake videos of famous people.
1. If anyone calls in our voice asking for money, ask for our family code word. No code word, no money.
2. Hang up and call back on the number you already have saved.
3. Never share an OTP, PIN or bank details on a call, even if the voice sounds like us.
4. A famous face promising to double your money is always fake.
5. When in doubt, wait 10 minutes and call one of us. Scammers hate waiting.

prompts.name: Make it in your family language
prompts.text: Rewrite this safety message in simple [Hindi / your language] for my parents, warm and short, keeping all 5 points: [paste the message above]

SAFE.tip: Agree the code word in person or on a call. Never post it, and never send it in the family group.

JOB.title: What AI can and can't do in your job: the 15-minute check
JOB.intro: AI takes tasks, not whole jobs. This prompt sorts your week into what to hand over, what to keep, and what to learn next.

prompts.name: The check
prompts.text:
My job: [title, industry, country].
Here are the tasks I did last week: [list 10 to 15 tasks with rough hours].
For each task, tell me: (a) can AI do most of it today, partly, or not really, and why in one line, (b) which free or common tool would help.
Then: the 3 tasks I should hand to AI first, the 3 parts of my job that are hardest to replace and why, and 2 skills to learn in the next 30 days to be worth more. Be honest, not reassuring.

prompts.name: The 30-day plan
prompts.text: Turn those 2 skills into a 30-day plan: 30 minutes a day, free resources only, one small proof I can show my manager at the end.

JOB.tip: Use real tasks from your calendar, not your job description. The answer is only as good as the list.

BOSS.title: 5 polite replies for after-hours messages
BOSS.intro: Short, friendly, and they don't start work at 11 pm. Plus a prompt to make your own.

prompts.name: Copy one
prompts.text:
1. Got it, I'll pick this up first thing tomorrow.
2. Thanks for flagging. I'll have it to you by [time] tomorrow.
3. Noted! I'm offline now, will look at it at 9.
4. On it tomorrow morning. Is anything here truly urgent tonight?
5. Sure. Can it wait till tomorrow, or should I flag it to [name] tonight?

prompts.name: Write your own
prompts.text: My boss messaged at [time]: "[message]". I want to reply kindly, not start work now, and give a clear time I will do it. Give me 3 options under 15 words each. No apologies.

BOSS.tip: Reply 4 is the quiet hero: it asks them to decide whether it is really urgent.

GIFT.title: The gift finder prompt
GIFT.intro: For bosses, in-laws and the cousin you barely know. A real shortlist inside your budget, not a smart watch that spies on them.

prompts.name: The prompt
prompts.text: Suggest 5 gift ideas for my [relation, e.g. boss], [age], who likes [2 or 3 things]. Occasion: [Diwali]. Budget: under [₹1,000] including delivery. City: [city]. Each idea: what it is, rough price, why it suits them, and one way it could go wrong. Nothing too personal for a [work / family] relationship.

prompts.name: The card
prompts.text: Write a 2-line card for this gift to my [relation]. Warm, not over the top, no more than 25 words.

GIFT.tip: Ask for "one way it could go wrong" every time. It catches the awkward gifts.

WISH.title: Diwali wishes that sound like you
WISH.intro: Personal wishes for a whole list of people in two minutes, without sounding like a forward or writing a book.

prompts.name: The prompt
prompts.text:
Write Diwali wishes for these people. Each one 1 or 2 short lines, in my voice (casual, warm, a little funny), using the one detail I give. No "sparkling", no "may this festival of lights", no emoji walls, max one emoji.
1. [Name] - [relation] - [one detail: a memory, a joke, what they did this year]
2. ...
3. ...

prompts.name: Mixed languages
prompts.text: Now write the same wishes in natural Hinglish, the way I would text them.

WISH.tip: The one detail per person is what makes it feel personal. Without it, you get a forward.

HIKE.title: The one-page wins list for your appraisal
HIKE.intro: Most people walk into an appraisal with nothing but a feeling. This turns your year into one page of wins with numbers, in about 20 minutes, using your own mail, calendar and notes.
steps: Search your sent mail for the last 12 months with words like done, shipped, launched, fixed, thank you, plus your manager's name.
Scroll your calendar for launches, reviews and client meetings you led.
Pick your 5 biggest wins and give each one a number: hours saved, customers, deadlines met, errors fixed.
Fit them on one page, then add one line on what you want to take on next year.
Bring any public salary survey only as context, and keep the tone calm and factual.

prompts.name: Find my wins
prompts.text: Here are notes and messages from my work this year: [paste, with confidential names and numbers removed]. Find the 5 biggest things I did. For each one, write a single line: what I did and the result, with a number if one is given. If there is no number, ask me for it instead of guessing. Do not invent anything.

prompts.name: Make it one page
prompts.text: Turn these 5 wins into a one-page appraisal summary in plain English, under 200 words, with no buzzwords and no headings except 'My year'. Wins: [paste].

prompts.name: Prepare the conversation
prompts.text: I have an appraisal meeting soon. My wins: [paste]. Write 3 short, calm sentences I can open with, then the 3 questions my manager is most likely to ask, each with an honest answer I could give. Keep it polite and confident, not pushy.

HIKE.tip: Don't paste confidential company data into a personal AI account. Remove client names and internal figures first.

SPACE.title: Free up your Google storage in 15 minutes
SPACE.intro: When the free 15 GB is full, photos stop backing up and your email can stop sending and receiving. Here is how to clear the biggest files first, for free.
steps: Back up anything precious first: download it, or export it with Google Takeout.
Open the Google storage manager (link below) and review 'Large items' first.
In Gmail, search has:attachment larger:10M, then delete the emails you don't need.
Delete old videos and screen recordings in Photos. They take far more space than pictures.
Empty the Bin in Gmail, Drive and Photos. Deleted files still count until the Bin is emptied.

prompts.name: Sort what to delete
prompts.text: I am freeing up storage. Here is a list of my largest files and emails with their sizes: [paste]. Sort them into three groups: safe to delete, check first, keep. Put anything that looks like an ID, a document or a family photo in 'keep' unless I say otherwise.

prompts.name: Build my search lines
prompts.text: Write 5 Gmail search lines that find big or old emails I can probably delete, for example newsletters or attachments older than 2 years. Use real Gmail operators such as has:attachment, larger:, older_than: and category:. Explain each one in a single short line.

SPACE.tip: Sort by size, not by date. Twenty big files free more space than two thousand small ones.

OFFER.title: Is this job offer real? The 10-minute check
OFFER.intro: Fake offers reach freshers and job hunters on WhatsApp and Telegram every day. Run these checks before you pay anything or share any documents.
steps: A fee to join, train or 'verify documents' is the biggest warning sign. Real employers do not charge one.
Look the company up for free on mca.gov.in under MCA Services, View Company/LLP Master Data (a free login may be needed). Check that the name, registered address and status match the letter.
Find the company's own website yourself and contact HR from there. Never use the number or link printed in the offer.
Be wary if the email comes from a free email address instead of the company's own domain.
No interview, pressure to pay today, or a recruiter who only chats? Stop there.
If you have paid or shared bank details, call 1930 or report at cybercrime.gov.in straight away.

prompts.name: Red flag check
prompts.text: Here is a job offer I received: [paste, with my personal details removed]. List every warning sign of a fake job offer that you can see in it, then list what I should verify myself on official sources. Do not tell me for certain that it is real or fake. Tell me what to check.

prompts.name: Ask HR to confirm
prompts.text: Write a short, polite email to a company's official HR address asking them to confirm whether this offer letter is genuine. Mention the role, the date on the letter and the name of the sender. Five lines maximum.

OFFER.tip: Treat any rush to pay as the scam itself. Real jobs wait while you check.

SCAM.title: The 60-second fake check: links, screenshots and PIN requests
SCAM.intro: Most money scams use one of three tricks: a link that promises free money, a fake 'payment done' screenshot, or a request for your PIN. Here is what to do with each one.
steps: A 'free money' or government bonus forward? Don't tap the link. Send it to PIB Fact Check on WhatsApp at +91 8799711259 or email factcheck@pib.gov.in. They check claims about the government.
Report the scam message or call on Chakshu, inside the Sanchar Saathi portal or app.
Selling online? Ship only when the money shows in your own bank or UPI app history. A screenshot can be edited.
Your UPI PIN is only for sending money. Nobody needs it for you to receive money.
If money has gone, call 1930 or report at cybercrime.gov.in at once.

prompts.name: Is this real?
prompts.text: Here is a message I received: [paste]. Do not tell me whether it is real. List the warning signs you can see, and tell me which official website or helpline I should use to check it myself.

prompts.name: Reply to the family group
prompts.text: Write a short, kind message for my family group saying this forward is fake and nobody should tap the link, without embarrassing the person who sent it. Three lines, simple English with a little Hindi.

prompts.name: Seller payment line
prompts.text: Write a friendly two-line message to a buyer saying that I ship as soon as the payment shows in my own account, and that I don't ship on screenshots.

SCAM.tip: Anything that rushes you ('today only', 'cut tonight', 'offer ends in 1 hour') is your cue to slow down.

JOBS.title: The free government job portal, set up in 15 minutes
JOBS.intro: National Career Service (NCS) is the Government of India's free job portal. Registering, searching and applying cost nothing at any stage, and it lists job fairs near you.
steps: Open ncs.gov.in and register as a Jobseeker with your mobile number and email.
Fill in your profile fully: education, skills and preferred city. Jobs are matched to it.
Search by role and location, and apply straight from the listing.
Open Events to find job fairs near you and register for the ones that fit.
Never pay anyone who says they are from NCS. The portal does not charge job seekers.

prompts.name: Match my CV to this job
prompts.text: Here is a job listing and my CV. List the 5 skills the listing asks for most, show where my CV already proves each one, and suggest one honest line I could add for any that are missing. Do not invent experience I don't have. Listing: [paste]. CV: [paste].

prompts.name: Why am I getting no replies?
prompts.text: I have applied to [number] jobs for [role] and got [number] replies. Here is my CV and 3 listings I applied to. Give me the 3 most likely reasons, in order, with one concrete change for each. Under 150 words, no headings.

prompts.name: Job fair in 10 minutes
prompts.text: I am going to a job fair for [role] in [city]. From my CV, write a 30-second introduction about me, then 5 questions an employer may ask, each with a short honest answer that uses only what is in my CV. CV: [paste].

JOBS.tip: Before you send any documents, check the job on the company's own careers page. Real employers never ask for a fee.

SIM.title: Check every SIM in your name, free, in 5 minutes
SIM.intro: Sanchar Saathi is the Department of Telecommunications' free portal and app. 'Know Your Mobile Connections' lists every mobile number registered with your ID and lets you report the ones that aren't yours.
steps: Open sancharsaathi.gov.in or the Sanchar Saathi app.
Choose 'Know Your Mobile Connections'.
Enter your mobile number and the captcha, then log in with the OTP sent to you.
Check the list. Mark any number you don't recognise as 'Not my number', and an old one you no longer use as 'Not required'.
Submit, and keep the reference ID to track your request.

prompts.name: Explain it to my parents
prompts.text: Write a short WhatsApp message in simple Hinglish for my parents. Explain in 4 numbered steps how to check how many SIMs are registered in their name on the government's Sanchar Saathi portal. End by reminding them never to read out an OTP to anyone who calls them.

prompts.name: My old numbers
prompts.text: Help me list every mobile number I may have used in the last 10 years: college, old jobs, data dongles, SIMs I bought for family. Ask me one question at a time, then give me a final list I can compare with the portal.

prompts.name: Read my result
prompts.text: The portal showed me these masked numbers: [paste]. For each one, help me work out whether it is my current number, an old one, or unknown, and which option fits: Required, Not required, or Not my number. Ask me questions instead of guessing.

SIM.tip: Do it for Mum and Papa too. Scammers often use older people's IDs.

PENSION.title: Papa's life certificate from home, free
PENSION.intro: Pensioners submit a life certificate (Jeevan Pramaan) once a year, mostly in November. The government's free face app lets them do it on an Android phone at home instead of in a bank queue.
steps: On an Android phone (Android 7 or newer), first install the AadhaarFaceRD app from the Play Store. It runs the face check.
Install the Jeevan Pramaan face app, using the link on jeevanpramaan.gov.in.
Keep ready: Papa's Aadhaar number, his mobile number, his PPO number and his pension bank account. His Aadhaar needs to be linked with his pension bank or office.
Sit him in good light, take the photo in the app, and have him blink when asked.
Keep the Pramaan ID that arrives by SMS. You can download the certificate on jeevanpramaan.gov.in.
Confirm his exact deadline with his bank or pension office.

prompts.name: Explain it to Papa
prompts.text: Write simple Hinglish steps for my father, who is not comfortable with phones, to submit his life certificate with the Jeevan Pramaan face app: install the two apps, keep his Aadhaar and PPO number ready, take the photo in good light and blink when asked. Short lines, one action per line.

prompts.name: Before we start
prompts.text: I am pasting the official Jeevan Pramaan FAQ: [paste]. Using only this text, make a short checklist of what we need before starting. Mark anything the text does not answer instead of guessing.

prompts.name: The fake pension call
prompts.text: Write a calm, short note for my father. The face app is free on his own phone. No bank or pension office will call and ask him to share an OTP or pay for his life certificate. If someone does, he should hang up and call his bank on the number printed in his passbook.

PENSION.tip: Do it early in the month. If the face check fails, try again in daylight and without glasses, or ask at his bank.

DOCS.title: Your marksheets, free, on DigiLocker
DOCS.intro: DigiLocker is the government's free document wallet. Many school boards and universities issue marksheets and certificates directly into it, and documents issued there are legally treated like the originals.
steps: Open digilocker.gov.in or the DigiLocker app and sign up with your Aadhaar-linked mobile number.
Go to Search Documents (or Education) and pick your board or university.
Enter your roll number and year exactly as they appear on the marksheet, then fetch the document.
It appears under Issued Documents. Download or share it for joining.
If your board or university isn't listed, apply for a duplicate on its official website, and tell HR the date you applied.

prompts.name: Email to HR
prompts.text: Write a short, polite email to HR. My original [marksheet] is not with me. I am sharing the DigiLocker issued copy now and will bring the original or the duplicate by [date]. Under 80 words. Do not use 'I hope this email finds you well'.

prompts.name: Joining checklist
prompts.text: Here is the document list from my joining letter: [paste]. Turn it into a checklist. For each item, say where I could get an official copy today. Mark anything you are unsure about instead of guessing.

prompts.name: Duplicate application
prompts.text: Write a short formal application to [board or university] asking for a duplicate [marksheet or certificate]. Roll number [x], year [y], reason: lost. Plain language, under 120 words.

DOCS.tip: Some employers still want to see the paper original later. Ask HR once, in writing, what they accept.

AUTOPAY.title: Find and stop every forgotten AutoPay
AUTOPAY.intro: Deleting an app does not stop its AutoPay. The mandate lives in your UPI app or your app store, and it keeps charging until you cancel it there. About 10 minutes, for you or your parents.
steps: Open each UPI app you have paid with (BHIM, Google Pay, PhonePe, Paytm or your bank's app) and find the AutoPay or Mandates section, usually under your profile or settings.
Tap each mandate you don't recognise or no longer use, choose Pause or Cancel, and follow the app's confirmation.
Check app-store subscriptions too. Android: Play Store > your profile > Payments and subscriptions > Subscriptions. iPhone: Settings > your name > Subscriptions.
Optional: NPCI's UPI Help (upihelp.npci.org.in) can show mandates across apps. It is still being rolled out, so if your bank isn't supported, use the app route above.
Next month, check your bank SMS or statement to confirm the charge stopped. If it continues after you cancelled, contact your bank through its official app or helpline.

prompts.name: Find the repeat charges
prompts.text: I'll paste 3 months of my bank SMS or statement lines (I have removed account and card numbers). List every charge that repeats, with the same amount or the same merchant, showing the dates and amounts. If you are not sure what a merchant is, write 'unknown' instead of guessing.

prompts.name: Explain it to Papa
prompts.text: Write a short WhatsApp message in simple Hinglish for my father. Explain that deleting an app does not stop its AutoPay, and give him the 3 steps to check the AutoPay section of his UPI app. Under 60 words, no jargon, warm tone.

prompts.name: Cancel in writing
prompts.text: Write a short, polite message to a company's customer support asking them to cancel my subscription [name] and confirm in writing that no further charges will be made. Under 70 words.

AUTOPAY.tip: No real company needs your UPI PIN to cancel a subscription over the phone. If someone calls offering to 'stop your AutoPay' for you, hang up and do it yourself in the app.

AADHAAR.title: Share your Aadhaar safely: the masked copy and the usage check
AADHAAR.intro: When someone asks for your Aadhaar on WhatsApp or email, you can often share the masked version, which shows only the last 4 digits. It's free on UIDAI's own site. Some official processes need the full number, so ask why before you send it.
steps: Go to myaadhaar.uidai.gov.in and log in with your Aadhaar number and the OTP sent to your registered mobile.
Choose Download Aadhaar and tick the masked Aadhaar option. The PDF shows only the last 4 digits.
Open the PDF with its password: the first 4 letters of your name in capitals plus your birth year (for example MEER1998).
In the same portal, open Authentication History to see when your Aadhaar was used. If you don't recognise something, call UIDAI on 1947.
Optional: use Lock/Unlock Biometrics so your fingerprint and iris can't be used until you unlock them.

prompts.name: Reply to HR
prompts.text: Write a short, polite reply to a recruiter who asked for my Aadhaar on WhatsApp. Say I'm happy to share a masked copy now, and the full copy through the company's official HR process after an offer. Under 50 words, friendly, not suspicious-sounding.

prompts.name: Is this request normal?
prompts.text: A company I applied to asked me for these documents: [list]. The stage I'm at: [first call / interview / offer / joining]. Tell me which of these are commonly asked at this stage, and which questions I should ask before sharing. Don't decide whether the company is real or fake; give me questions I can check.

prompts.name: Check the recruiter's message
prompts.text: Here is a recruiter's message: [paste]. List any red flags (a personal email address, urgency, payment requests, ID requests before any interview) and anything that looks normal. Be brief and specific.

AADHAAR.tip: Before sending any ID photo, write across it with your phone's markup tool: 'For [company] job application only, [date]'. That makes the copy harder to reuse somewhere else.

LOST.title: Phone lost or stolen: the first 30 minutes
LOST.intro: Do these in order from a laptop or a borrowed phone. All of them are free.
steps: Secure it first. Android: google.com/android/find. iPhone: icloud.com/find. Lock it or mark it as lost. Erase it only if you won't get it back, because erasing can stop you from locating it.
From another phone, call your mobile operator to block the SIM, then get a replacement SIM on the same number at their store.
Call your bank's official helpline (the number is on the back of your card or on the bank's website) to block UPI and cards on the lost phone.
File a police complaint (many states let you report a lost phone online) and keep the complaint number.
Block the phone's IMEI on Sanchar Saathi: Block Your Lost/Stolen Mobile. You'll need the IMEI (on the box or bill), the complaint number and your number.
If money has already gone, call 1930 or report at cybercrime.gov.in straight away.

prompts.name: My next hour
prompts.text: My phone was just lost or stolen. It had these apps: [list]. Make me a short, numbered checklist for the next hour, in order of urgency. Don't invent helpline numbers; tell me where to find each one officially.

prompts.name: Complaint draft
prompts.text: Write a clear, factual police complaint for a lost or stolen phone using these details: [phone model, IMEI, number, date, time, place, what happened]. Plain English, under 150 words.

prompts.name: Passwords to change
prompts.text: I lost my phone. I use these accounts on it: [list]. Tell me which passwords to change first and why, starting with my email. Keep it short.

LOST.tip: Do this today, before you need it: dial *#06# to see your IMEI and save it in your email.

CLEAN.title: WhatsApp storage: free up gigabytes in 10 minutes
CLEAN.intro: WhatsApp keeps every forwarded photo and video. Clear the big files without losing your chats, then stop them coming back.
steps: WhatsApp > Settings > Storage and data > Manage storage. Start with 'Forwarded many times' and 'Larger than 5 MB'.
Open the biggest chats (they are sorted by size), select the media you don't need and delete it. Your messages stay; only the files go.
Stop new files piling up: Settings > Storage and data > Media auto-download, and set it to No media (or Wi-Fi only).
For a busy group, open group info and set Media visibility to No (Android) or Save to Photos to Never (iPhone), so its files stay out of your gallery.
Your backup can be huge too: Settings > Chats > Chat backup, and switch off Include videos if you don't need them backed up.

prompts.name: Explain it to Mum
prompts.text: Write a short Hinglish WhatsApp message for my mum explaining how to free WhatsApp storage: Settings, Storage and data, Manage storage, then delete 'Forwarded many times'. Under 60 words, friendly, no jargon.

prompts.name: A kind note to the family group
prompts.text: Write a light, warm message for our family WhatsApp group suggesting we share photos in one shared album instead of sending them one by one, without offending anyone. Under 40 words.

CLEAN.tip: Check your Photos or Gallery app for a WhatsApp folder too. Deleting files in WhatsApp's own storage tool is the cleanest way, because it removes them in one place.

PASSBOOK.title: Is your PF really deposited? The 10-minute passbook check
PASSBOOK.intro: Your payslip shows what was cut. Your EPFO passbook shows what actually arrived. You can check it yourself, free, without asking anyone.
steps: Find your UAN (12 digits) on your payslip, or ask HR for it.
First time? Activate your UAN on the EPFO member portal with the mobile number registered with EPFO.
Log in at passbook.epfindia.gov.in with your UAN and password, then pick the member ID for your current employer.
Check that every month has both an employee share and an employer share, and match them against your payslips.
A month missing for a long time? Raise a grievance at epfigms.gov.in and keep the reference number. The UMANG app shows the passbook too.

prompts.name: Payslip vs passbook table
prompts.text: I'll paste the PF figures from my payslips and the entries from my EPFO passbook for the same months. Make a simple table with these columns: month, PF on payslip, employee share in passbook, employer share in passbook. Mark any month that is missing or doesn't match. Do not guess any number I didn't give you.

prompts.name: Polite note to HR
prompts.text: Write a short, polite message to my HR team about my PF for these months: [months]. My payslips show it deducted, but my EPFO passbook doesn't show the deposit yet. Ask when it will be credited. Under 80 words, friendly, no blame.

prompts.name: Explain my passbook
prompts.text: Here is a line from my EPFO passbook: [paste, remove your UAN]. Explain in plain words what each column means. If you are not sure what a column means, say so instead of guessing.

PASSBOOK.tip: Deposits can take a few weeks to show, so look for months that stay missing. If your company runs its own PF trust, the EPFO passbook may not show your balance. Ask HR for the trust's statement instead.

CODE.title: Lock your WhatsApp in 2 minutes, before someone asks for 'the code'
CODE.intro: The 6-digit WhatsApp code is the key to your account. Anyone who asks for it, even from a friend's or relative's number, is trying to log in as you and ask your contacts for money.
steps: The family rule: never send the 6-digit WhatsApp code to anyone, even if a known number asks for it.
Open WhatsApp > Settings > Account > Two-step verification > Turn on.
Set a 6-digit PIN only you know (not 123456 or a birthday), and add an email so you can reset it.
If a friend asks you for a code, phone them on a normal call first. Their WhatsApp may already have been taken.
If your account is taken, open WhatsApp and verify your number again on your own phone, warn your contacts not to send money to messages in your name, and report it at 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in.

prompts.name: Family group message
prompts.text: Write a short WhatsApp message for my family group in simple Hinglish. Explain two things: never send the 6-digit WhatsApp code to anyone, even a relative's number, and how to turn on two-step verification (Settings, Account, Two-step verification). Under 60 words, warm, not scary.

prompts.name: Step by step for Papa
prompts.text: Explain to my 65-year-old father, one tiny step at a time, how to turn on two-step verification in WhatsApp. First ask which phone he has and wait for the answer before giving any steps.

prompts.name: Is this message a trick?
prompts.text: Here is a message I got: [paste, remove personal details]. Does it ask me for a code, PIN, OTP or money? List any warning signs in plain words. If you can't be sure, tell me to call the person on a normal call to check.

CODE.tip: Your PIN and the 6-digit code are both yours alone. WhatsApp itself may ask for your PIN now and then to check it's you, and that is normal. A person asking for either one is not.

PASSWORD.title: Find your leaked passwords, free, in 10 minutes
PASSWORD.intro: If one password opens 14 apps, one leak opens all 14. Your phone can already tell you which of your saved passwords have shown up in data leaks.
steps: On Android or Chrome, open passwords.google.com and sign in.
Tap Password Checkup > Check passwords. Fix Compromised first, then Reused, then Weak.
On iPhone, open the Passwords app (Settings > Passwords on older versions) and look under Security for leaked and reused passwords.
Change the leaked ones first, starting with your email, because email can reset everything else.
Turn on 2-Step Verification for your Google account at myaccount.google.com/security.

prompts.name: My change-first list
prompts.text: I'll list the apps and sites I use, with no passwords. Sort them into the order I should change passwords in, starting with accounts that can reset others, like email. Just the list, one line each.

prompts.name: A passphrase I'll remember
prompts.text: Explain how to make a long passphrase from 4 random everyday words that I can remember. Give me the method and one example that I must not use. Never ask me for my real password.

prompts.name: Is this login alert real?
prompts.text: I got this 'new sign-in' alert: [paste, remove personal details]. Tell me how to check it safely by opening the app or website myself, not by tapping any link in the message.

PASSWORD.tip: Never type a real password into any AI chat. The checkers above run inside your own account.

UNDO.title: The reply-all rescue: 30 seconds to unsend
UNDO.intro: Gmail gives you only 5 seconds to undo a send by default. One setting makes every email wait 30 seconds, so you can catch the wrong 'To' line before anyone sees it.
steps: In Gmail on a computer, click the gear > See all settings.
In the General tab, find Undo Send and choose 30 seconds.
Scroll to the bottom and click Save Changes.
In Outlook on the web, go to Settings > Mail > Compose and reply > Undo send, and move the slider to the maximum.
For any angry or private email, write it first and add the To line last.

prompts.name: Before I send
prompts.text: Read this email before I send it: [paste]. Tell me in 3 lines: who it seems written for, anything that would embarrass me if the whole office read it, and one calmer line I could use instead. Don't rewrite the rest.

prompts.name: The short sorry
prompts.text: I sent an email to the wrong group by mistake. Write a 2-line, calm follow-up saying 'please ignore the earlier email, sent in error'. No long apology, and no 'I hope this email finds you well'.

prompts.name: Reply-all check
prompts.text: Before I reply-all, here are the roles of everyone on this thread: [paste roles, not names]. Should this reply go to everyone or to one person? Answer in one line.

UNDO.tip: Undo only works while the email is still waiting. Once the timer runs out it has gone, so send a two-line 'please ignore' rather than a long apology.
